name: Glycolic acid

lead: Glycolic acid is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid and one of the most widely used chemical exfoliants. People use it for dullness, rough texture, dark spots, acne marks and fine lines, in home products and professional peels.

It weakens the bonds between surface skin cells so dull cells shed faster, and with repeated use it stimulates epidermal renewal and has been reported to increase dermal collagen. Trials show modest improvements in texture and photoaging, and a 2024 systematic review of chemical peels for melasma (24 studies, 1,075 participants) concluded glycolic acid was the most safe and effective peeling agent among those studied.

paras: At home it comes as toners, serums and pads used a few nights a week, with sunscreen by day. Stronger peels are done in clinics. Users often debate strength and frequency, and glow and texture changes show up over weeks of regular use.

Stinging, redness and peeling are common, and skin becomes more sensitive to sunlight, so sunscreen is advised. Excess strength or poor technique can cause burns and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin tones. Peel depth is linked to both results and complications.

angle.text: Glycolic acid is used as an exfoliant for dullness, rough texture, dark spots, acne marks and fine lines. It loosens dead surface skin so cells shed faster and skin looks smoother and brighter. Trials show modest texture and photoaging gains; stronger products commonly irritate.

lead: Glycolic acid (hydroxyacetic acid, HOCH2COOH) is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid (AHA) and one of the most widely used chemical exfoliants for improving how skin looks. Applied to the face, it loosens the bonds between dead surface cells so they shed, which people use to smooth rough texture, brighten dull skin, unclog pores and fade uneven pigmentation. It is found in daily cleansers, toners, pads and serums at low strength, and in higher-strength peels applied by clinicians.[1][2][3][4]

The chain people describe runs from exfoliation to skin that reflects light more evenly: shedding the outer layer of dead cells smooths texture and lets products and makeup sit better, repeated use is said to ease clogged pores and acne marks, and professional courses of peels are used for sun-related roughness, fine lines and patchy pigmentation such as melasma.[2][5][6] A 2024 systematic review of chemical peels for melasma, covering 24 studies with 1,075 participants, concluded that glycolic acid was the safest and most effective peeling agent among those studied, although the studies were too varied to pool.[5]

The compound occurs naturally in sugarcane, sugar beets, pineapple and unripe grapes, and is produced industrially for cosmetics, textiles and biodegradable polymers.[1][1] Its skin-care use dates to AHA research by Van Scott and Yu, who reported in 1974 that AHAs affect keratinization disorders and peel skin with minimal risk.[3] Dermatology reviews describe glycolic acid peeling as a superficial resurfacing treatment, and a 1996 editorial in Dermatologic Surgery already discussed it as an established procedure.[6][7]

Glycolic acid is an irritant. Reviews and product labels describe stinging, redness and peeling as common, and regulators advise sun protection because AHAs can raise sensitivity to ultraviolet light.[8][9] Peel depth is linked in the literature to both results and complications.[6]

paras: Glycolic acid is sold in cleansers, toners, pads, serums and leave-on treatments aimed at dullness, rough texture, clogged pores and signs of photoaging. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes concentrations of 5 to 10 percent in cosmetics as promoting epidermal renewal and improving texture and tone.[10] Professional peels use higher concentrations and are applied by clinicians; reviews describe them as superficial resurfacing procedures.[6][2]

A narrative review of glycolic acid peel therapy lists the main indications as acne and acne scarring, melasma, photoaging (roughness and fine wrinkles), and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and describes it as suitable for lighter to medium skin tones when patients are carefully selected.[2] Wikipedia's chemical peel article places AHAs at the mildest end of peel agents, used for light peels, with TCA at medium depth and phenol-croton oil at deep.[4]

In pigmentation, a 2024 review describes glycolic acid among peeling agents used as additional or maintenance therapy for melasma.[11] A review of striae distensae (stretch marks) lists it among commonly cited topical treatments alongside tretinoin and ascorbic acid, while noting the lack of strong evidence for any treatment.[12]

Clinic protocols described in the literature often prime skin with topical retinoids or hydroquinone beforehand, run a series of peels spaced a couple of weeks apart over several months, and finish with sun protection. The Sharad review gives this as one clinician's regimen rather than a standard, and notes that combining peels with microneedling or topical therapy has been studied for acne scars and melasma.[2]

At home, products are typically used a couple of times a week and built up gradually, a pattern echoed in the use directions on a retail glycolic acid pad label.[8] Glycolic acid is often discussed alongside other exfoliating acids such as lactic, mandelic, citric and salicylic acid.[13][14]

As a keratolytic, glycolic acid weakens the cohesion between corneocytes, the flattened cells of the outer skin layer, so that desquamation (shedding) speeds up. Its small molecular size is described as aiding penetration.[2][3][10]

Beyond exfoliation, Sharad's review lists anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, and histology in photoaging studies showing thinner stratum corneum and thicker epidermis after peeling.[2] A 2021 laboratory study on skin explants from a single donor, funded by the manufacturer ISDIN, found that glycolic acid gels and creams adjusted to pH 4 raised total collagen by roughly 5 to 10 percent at 8 to 25 percent concentration without changing TNF-alpha expression.[15]

A 2018 review in Molecules by Tang and Yang describes AHAs as having dual effects that depend on concentration: low concentrations were associated with reduced UVB-induced inflammatory signals in cell experiments, while higher concentrations increased reactive oxygen species and cell death under UVB.[3]

Peel intensity depends on concentration, formulation pH and contact time. Unbuffered solutions can have a very low pH, and buffered or partially neutralised forms are considered safer; clinicians stop the acid's action by neutralising or rinsing at a set point.[2][6]

Human research includes a 2024 systematic review of 24 melasma peel studies (9 clinical or comparative trials and 15 randomized controlled trials, 1,075 participants in total, 8 to 36 weeks), which named glycolic acid the safest and most effective peeling agent.[5] In the Sharad review, one melasma study reported 91 percent of patients improved on the MASI score with 50 percent glycolic acid, and trichloroacetic acid worked faster but had a higher relapse rate (25 percent versus 5.9 percent).[2]

For acne, the same review reports a 90 percent response in one study using 35 to 50 percent glycolic acid, better tolerability than Jessner's solution with similar efficacy, and in a split-face trial better sustained results with salicylic acid.[2] For atrophic acne scars, 70 percent glycolic acid peels every other week outperformed daily 15 percent glycolic acid cream in one study.[2] For photoaging, 50 percent peels improved mild roughness and fine wrinkles, but deep wrinkles and deep pigmentation were not affected.[2]

A 2009 study examined topical glycolic acid and salicylic acid in relation to ultraviolet-induced erythema, DNA damage and sunburn cell formation in human skin.[16] The FDA reports industry-sponsored studies in which four weeks of AHA use raised sensitivity to UV-induced redness by about 18 percent and roughly doubled sensitivity to UV-induced cellular damage on average, reversible within a week of stopping.[9]

Other trials include a 2000 randomized trial of hydroquinone cream with or without salicylic acid peels for photodamage of the neck and chest, which tested salicylic rather than glycolic acid,[17] and a 2025 randomized trial of an AGE-inhibiting moisturizer's effect on procedure effectiveness.[18] Registered trials include a single 70 percent glycolic acid peel with vitamin C for photoaging and for acne scars (10 participants each), a withdrawn trial of glycolic-salicylic versus glycolic peel for melasma, a pilot comparison of salicylic and glycolic peels in melasma, a trial of modified Jessner's solution or glycolic acid with trichloroacetic acid in melasma, and a study in acquired epidermodysplasia verruciformis in HIV-infected children.[19][20][21][22][23][24]

Wikipedia characterizes glycolic acid as a skin irritant and lists corrosive hazard statements for the concentrated substance.[1] The common effects of AHA peels are erythema, stinging, burning, a pulling sensation and transient post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; unbuffered solutions can cause erosive blisters and scarring, and rare events include hypopigmentation, persistent redness and one reported case of contact urticaria.[2][4]

The FDA received 114 adverse dermatologic reports for AHA skin-care products between 1992 and February 2004, mostly burning, rash and swelling, with serious reactions occurring most often with the most exfoliating products such as skin peelers.[9] In January 2005 it recommended a 'Sunburn Alert' on AHA cosmetics advising sunscreen, protective clothing and limited sun exposure during use and for a week afterwards.[9] A retail glycolic acid pad label in DailyMed carries external-use-only warnings, advises stopping if irritation develops, advises against broken skin, suggests starting once or twice weekly, and advises SPF 30 or higher.[8]

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded, according to the FDA, that glycolic and lactic acid products are safe at 10 percent or less with a pH of 3.5 or higher and sun protection.[9] Taiwan's health ministry has raised safety concerns about 20 to 70 percent low-pH AHA peels, according to the Molecules review.[3] The Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology review of superficial and medium-depth peels states that peel depth is directly related to both results and complications.[6]

Sharad's review says epidermolysis risk rises with recent retinoids, anti-acne agents or skin lighteners, excessive scrubbing and pre-existing dryness, and that sun exposure afterwards can cause hyperpigmentation.[2] Grokipedia also notes that ingesting ethylene glycol produces glycolic acid and oxalate with kidney risk, which concerns systemic exposure rather than cosmetic use.[10]

Glycolic acid is slightly stronger than acetic acid because of its electron-withdrawing hydroxyl group, with a pKa near 3.8.[1][10] It is produced industrially mainly by catalysed carbonylation of formaldehyde, and also from chloroacetic acid and sodium hydroxide.[1] It occurs in all green plants as a by-product of photorespiration.[1] It is also a monomer for polyglycolic acid and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), biodegradable polymers with a large separate literature on drug delivery and implants.[1][25]

Auguste Laurent coined the name in 1848, proposing it as the acid corresponding to glycine. Adolph Strecker and Nikolai Sokolov first prepared it in 1851.[1] Chemical peeling itself dates to 19th-century dermatology, when Ferdinand von Hebra used agents such as phenol and croton oil, and mainstream phenol peeling followed in the 1960s.[4]

In 1974 Van Scott and Yu reported that AHAs could treat keratinization disorders and peel skin with minimal risk, opening the way for AHA cosmetics and peels.[3] A 1996 editorial in Dermatologic Surgery already discussed glycolic acid peels as an established procedure, and a 2013 review summarised the clinical literature.[7][2]

Glycolic acid features in fitness-forum discussion mostly in passing, as one of the cheap, widely sold exfoliating actives. On T Nation, a poster in a life-tips thread says skin products containing AHAs such as lactic, malic and glycolic acid make skin look noticeably better, and another comments that creams with retinoids or glycolic acid carry heavy markups.[14][26]
Its safety profile has drawn regulatory attention: the FDA's AHA guidance and the cosmetic industry's expert panel set out the concentration, pH and sun-protection conditions described above.[9]
